messages.subject: Accounting for trapping effort openCR
parts:
Hi Murray and all,

I’m running openCR on rock wallaby trapping data that spans several years. I’m trying to adjust for trapping effort as best as I can and I wanted to see if my current method and estimates can be improved on.

I’m using trapping data ranging from 2014 to 2021, and in the earlier years they would commonly set one trap twice in one night, whereby they set and processed the same trap in the evening and early morning. This would allow two opportunities for a wallaby to be trapped at that trap location in that one night.

To model this, I made two separate traps at the same location (jittered the points so they were only 1m apart). I would then close that second trap at the location if they had only set it once that night. In 2021, they would only set traps up once on the night and so essentially 2021 is approximately half the trapping effort of those earlier trapping years.

My first question; is this method the best way to model this trapping scenario?

My second question; is using ‘single’ as the detector type the best option vs ‘multi’?
I will usually put multi as there are examples of multiple animals (2 max) getting caught in the same trap in my data, however, I’m not sure if this would influence trapping effort as I’ve run them both and they appear not to make a difference to my results.

My third; is there any other ways to account for this variable trapping effort?

There are concerns that the decrease in estimates in 2021 (figure below using openCR estimates) is due to trapping effort rather than true abundance. I’ve also been told that estimates in the last session of your model will naturally drop? Is this correct?

Any advice would be greatly appreciated.   

I’ve also run a non-spatial CR with the openCR package just to compare the results (figure below). I’m used to non-spatial models showing lower estimates than spatial models, however, the pattern observed below is a little all over the place.

 

Thanks!

Kristen

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Accounting for trapping effort openCR
parts:
Hello Kristen
I don't pretend to have definitive answers, but here are some thoughts.

1. Your description 'set and processed the same trap in the evening and early morning' seems to describe two distinct capture occasions, rather like the am and pm occasions of the Coulombe house mouse dataset in Otis et al. 1978. I'm assuming the traps were opened for just a few hours at each time to minimize stress on the animals (I once helped briefly with a YFRW study like that). If so then I would think it simpler to just enter the data as occasion-specific, rather than injecting supernumerary traps and turning them off and on (presumably with 'usage'). You might want to consider an occasion-specific covariate am vs pm. But I doubt these fiddles will make a noticeable difference to the estimates.

Your two-trap approach has the problem that 'trapping' implies a maximum of one capture per occasion per animal, whereas a wallaby might be caught both evening and morning, at least in principle.

2. The 'single' option is treated the same as 'multi' in practice, because there is no probability model for the single-catch case (we approximate with 'multi', expecting good density estimates but biased g0-hat or lambda0-hat). For each closed population you can fit a single-catch model with the 'simulation and inverse-prediction' method in the new package 'ipsecr', but that is sort of academic and unnecessary.

3. Other ways - not really. For non-trapping data ('proximity' and 'count' detectors) you can allow for the duration of detector opening in the usage attribute, but that doesn't properly represent what is going on (wallaby caught at most once on each occasion).

Regarding the plot: Jolly-Seber estimates in the last (and first) session of a non-spatial series are strongly biased down by individual heterogeneity - the classic references are by Gilbert and by Carothers from the early 1970s. I guess that might also happen with spatial data when there is unmodelled heterogeneity, but I haven't investigated and would expect a smaller effect. The jump in 2016 also needs explaining.

If you have robust-design data (multiple trapping occasions in each year) then why not add a plot of the closed-population spatial estimates? I am a bit unsure about using open spatial estimates for density, as they may be affected by the choice of model structures for survival and recruitment. Something like fits <- lapply(ch, secr.fit, buffer = 500, etc.) will do it. Then fits <- secrlist(fits); predict(fits)

Cheers
Murray
